extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and media readers interested in journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating a journalist's plagiarism incident and the appropriate editorial response, including causes, apologies, sanctions, and lessons for newsroom practice. Focuses on ethical standards and practical safeguards against improper use of others' reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism is a cardinal sin in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism — using another newspaper's work 'as if it were my own' — is described as 'one of the cardinal sins in journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material 'borrowed and duplicated, without attribution' is unacceptable; reporters must not present others' reporting as their own. The page uses the Washington Post/Arizona Republic episode as an example of substantive material being copied into Post stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apologize and accept responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The wrongdoer should issue an abject apology and accept responsibility and punishment ('I am deeply sorry... I accept the punishment that the Washington Post has given to me').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apology that names the offense, expresses remorse, accepts sanction, and promises to improve is presented as the correct public response by a journalist who has committed plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline pressure is not an adequate excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that plagiarism arose 'under the pressure of tight deadlines' are noted but viewed skeptically — deadlines are not new for veteran reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that while deadline pressure is often cited, it does not justify cutting corners, especially for experienced journalists; responsibility remains with the reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain careful note-taking and separate source text
rubrics_metrics.description: Faulty note-taking or putting somebody else's words on your screen and later conflating them with your own notes can lead to accidental plagiarism (example: Ruth Shalit; Doris Kearns Goodwin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical safeguard: do not paste source text into documents of personal notes without clear attribution; keep downloaded/source material and one's own notes clearly separated to avoid conflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizations should review past work for patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should examine a reporter's previous writing to determine whether plagiarism is an isolated incident or part of a pattern (the Post 'did a review of her previous writing and found no other examples').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clean prior record is relevant to disciplinary decisions and public judgement about the incident's severity and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions should be proportionate and consider career record
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions between suspension and firing should weigh the reporter's overall record and whether the behavior is 'out of character' (the Post suspended Horwitz for three months rather than firing her).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author favors second chances for otherwise exemplary reporters when the misconduct appears isolated; punishment proportionality is highlighted as an evaluative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in public apologies and disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers expect clear communication about what happened; the Post's apology initially 'didn't name the offending reporter or say what her punishment was,' which the author found puzzling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice implied: apologies and institutional statements should be sufficiently transparent about the nature of the misconduct and the corrective action to inform the public and preserve trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the cause publicly so the profession can learn
rubrics_metrics.description: The author requests that the reporter 'tell us what happened so that other journalists -- and bloggers -- can learn from your mistake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond apology, a candid explanation of how the lapse occurred (e.g., note-taking failure vs. deliberate cutting of corners) is framed as valuable for community learning and prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish accidental from deliberate misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece considers whether the incident was accidental (confused notes) or deliberate (cutting corners) and treats the distinction as important for judgment and sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should seek evidence about intent; explanations based on confusion have been advanced in past cases but are often questioned by critics—intent affects both moral assessment and personnel decisions.
